opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the core issue is that a lot of these companies are building for the models of today rather than the models of two years from now. If you look at the trendlines (effective compute going up roughly half an order of magnitude a year, plus algorithmic efficiencies, plus what I'd call the "unhobbling" gains), the models are just going to get dramatically better, and fast.

A lot of wrapper companies are essentially building scaffolding to paper over the current limitations of the models. The model can't do long-horizon tasks, so you build some elaborate agent framework. The model hallucinates in a certain domain, so you build a retrieval pipeline and a bunch of guardrails. The model doesn't have context on your workflow, so you build an integration layer. Those are real problems today, but a lot of that value gets steamrolled by the next generation of models. The labs themselves are working on exactly those unhobblings: longer context, better tool use, test-time compute, models that can actually act as agents over days or weeks.

So the thing I keep coming back to is the drop-in remote worker. If in a few years you have a model that can onboard like a new employee, read your Slack, use your computer, and do the job, then a bunch of these narrow vertical products, the "AI for legal intake" or "AI for writing marketing emails," are just a subset of what the general system does out of the box. The value accrues to whoever has the best model and the compute, not to the thin layer on top.

There are exceptions, to be fair. If you have real proprietary data, real distribution, deep integration into some regulated workflow, or a hard-to-replicate customer relationship, that can be durable. But the "we put a nice UI on the API and wrote some clever prompts" companies? I think a lot of people are underrating how quickly that moat erodes. It's a bit like building a business in 2005 around the specific limitations of dial-up internet. The ground is shifting under you, and the rate of change is the thing people consistently underestimate.

r001.rationale: The response says a future drop-in remote-worker model would handle tasks covered by narrow vertical products out of the box, eroding the value of wrapper offerings.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, the core thing is that the value is going to accrue to whoever controls the frontier models, and the wrappers are basically renting a moat they don't own. Every six to twelve months the labs ship a new model, and whatever clever scaffolding you built to paper over the last model's weaknesses just gets eaten. You spent a year building retrieval pipelines and prompt chains and agent loops to make GPT-4 do something reliably, and then the next model just does it natively. Your product becomes a feature, or worse, it becomes nothing.

And I think people underestimate how fast this is going to go. We're not talking about incremental improvements. If you buy the trend lines, effective compute is scaling something like half an order of magnitude a year, plus algorithmic progress on top of that, plus unhobbling. So the models in 2027 aren't going to be slightly better chatbots. They're going to be something closer to drop-in remote workers. In that world, the thin layer of UI and workflow logic you've wrapped around the API is just not where the leverage is.

There's also the structural point. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, they're all going to go up the stack themselves. They have the model, they have the distribution, they have the data on what users actually want, and they have a very strong incentive to capture the margin. A wrapper company is competing with its own supplier. That's historically a terrible position to be in.

Now, I want to be a little careful. There are things that look like wrappers but aren't, because they own something the labs can't easily get. Proprietary data, deep integration into some regulated industry, real distribution with enterprise customers who are slow to switch. Those can be real businesses. But a lot of what got funded in 2023 and 2024 was "ChatGPT for X" where the only moat was that you got there first. And "first" doesn't mean much when the underlying capability improves ten-x in two years.

So the way I'd put it is, if your business thesis depends on the models staying roughly as dumb as they are today, you're betting against the single most reliable trend of the decade. That's the bet I'm bearish on.

r001.rationale: The response says that improving models will become “drop-in remote workers” and that capabilities wrappers provide will be absorbed by the models, leaving wrapper products as features or obsolete.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic problem is that you’re building on a capability that’s changing incredibly quickly, and you don’t control that change. You can build a useful product around something the models don’t quite do today. But then the next generation comes out, and suddenly a lot of what you built is something the model can do directly.

Imagine you’ve spent a year building scaffolding to get a model to perform some particular task reliably. You’ve got all these prompts, you’ve got a retrieval system, you’ve got a workflow that compensates for its weaknesses. That can create real value today. But how much of that work survives when the underlying model gets substantially better?

The other question is who captures the value. You’re dependent on a few model providers, and those providers also have an incentive to build applications. Meanwhile, your competitors have access to essentially the same intelligence you do. So you need some reason customers will choose you and stay with you beyond having a clever way to call the API.

There will be valuable businesses here. Distribution, deep integration into a customer’s workflow, proprietary data—those can matter a lot. I’m bearish on the idea that putting an interface around a model is, by itself, a durable business. You want to ask: if the model gets ten times better, does my company become more valuable, or does the reason it exists disappear?

r001.rationale: The response says improved models may perform tasks directly and make wrapper scaffolding obsolete, but it does not connect this to models acting as drop-in remote workers.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic worry is that you’re building a company on a capability gap that the next model release might close. You spend six months getting a model to do something reliably, with a bunch of scaffolding and prompt engineering, and then the next generation just does it out of the box. Your product gets better, but your competitive advantage disappears.

And the model companies are going to move into applications. They have the distribution, they have the best access to the models, and they can optimize the models for their own products. If your pitch is essentially “ChatGPT, but with a slightly better interface for this particular task,” that’s a pretty precarious position.

That doesn’t mean there won’t be valuable application companies. If you own the customer relationship, you’re deeply embedded in a workflow, or you have some proprietary data that actually matters, there could be a real business there. But you have to ask: as the models get dramatically better, does your moat get stronger, or does the reason your company exists go away?

r001.rationale: The response says newer models may close capability gaps and erase a wrapper’s competitive advantage, but it does not describe models becoming capable of acting as drop-in remote workers.
